interest: This collection offers valuable insight into the tightening economic friction and wartime mobilization between Japan and the United States on the eve of the Pacific War. It illustrates both formal fiscal adjustments through the revision of Japan's Income Tax Law in 1940 and the administrative mechanisms used to restrict capital flight and monitor individuals through mandatory tax clearance certificates prior to foreign departure in late 1941. Furthermore, the memoranda regarding Japan's accelerated gold shipments illuminate Japan's desperate bid to convert specie reserves into American raw materials and manufactures before the expiration of the 1911 commercial treaty, revealing how State Department analysts like Stanley K. Hornbeck independently verified and monitored the depletion of Japan's secret gold reserves.
keywords: Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1911
overview: This file comprises State Department records from 1940 and 1941 primarily classified under decimal file 894.5123 (Japanese taxation and financial conditions), along with related economic intelligence on gold reserves and exports. The documents include a diplomatic despatch from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo transmitting a translated revision of Japan's 1940 Income Tax Law; cross-reference sheets from late 1941 detailing tax clearance requirements and financial exit restrictions imposed on foreigners departing Japan and reciprocal income tax compliance rules for Japanese agents departing the United States; and memoranda by Stanley K. Hornbeck and the Division of Far Eastern Affairs evaluating consular reports from Kobe on Japan's accelerated gold exports and depleted Bank of Japan gold reserves preceding the termination of the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation.

subfiles.about: Transmits an English translation of Japan's Law No. 24 of 1940, which revised the Japanese Income Tax Law, for forwarding to the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce.
subfiles.from: George A. Makinson, First Secretary of Embassy, Tokyo
keywords: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.summary: American Embassy Tokyo despatch No. 5056 forwards an English translation made by the Okuyama Service of Law No. 24, revising the Income Tax Law of Japan as published in the Official Gazette of March 29, 1940. First Secretary George A. Makinson explains that the Commercial Attaché's office customarily provides such statutory translations to the Finance Division of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce. The document is routed through the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs and Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5056 from Embassy Tokyo Enclosing Translation of Japanese Income Tax Law No. 24

subfiles.about: Notes that foreigners departing Japan must present receipts showing payment of income taxes and other financial obligations before obtaining exit permits.
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference file note referencing a British Embassy despatch of September 8, 1941, originally filed under decimal file 894.56/82. It summarizes Japanese regulations requiring foreigners leaving Japan to obtain receipts proving payment of income taxes for the current financial year (which would normally not be assessed until the following April). Departing foreigners were also required to prove settlement of rent, staff gratuities, and retiring allowances at prescribed Japanese rates prior to receiving an exit permit.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet Regarding Tax and Exit Clearance Requirements for Foreigners Leaving Japan

subfiles.about: Records that departing Japanese agents in the United States must provide certificates of compliance for income tax payments but not other taxes.
subfiles.from: Schuler, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet referencing a memorandum dated September 16, 1941, by Schuler in the Division of Far Eastern Affairs (filed under 894.56/82). It notes that Japanese agents departing the United States were required to submit a certificate of compliance demonstrating payment of U.S. income tax. It clarifies that this compliance certificate requirement applied exclusively to income taxes and was not mandated for other taxes.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet Concerning Income Tax Compliance Certificates for Japanese Agents Leaving the United States

subfiles.about: Highlights intelligence from Consul Gourley in Kobe regarding accelerated Japanese gold exports to the United States and the depletion of Japan's gold reserves.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.summary: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck to the Secretary of State highlighting two points of critical interest from a report by Consul Louis H. Gourley at Kobe. Hornbeck explains that Japan accelerated gold exports to the United States during late 1939 to purchase commodities prior to the expiration of the 1911 commercial treaty. He further emphasizes that Japan's true gold reserve had fallen to approximately 369,780,000 yen ($120,000,000), a figure corroborating independent calculations made within the Department of State by Mr. Luthringer.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck on Japanese Gold Shipments and Bank of Japan Gold Reserves

subfiles.about: Analyzes Consul Gourley's report on Japan's accelerated gold exports during late 1939 and the discrepancy between official and estimated Bank of Japan gold reserves.
subfiles.from: Jones, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing a report from Consul Louis H. Gourley in Kobe regarding Japanese gold shipments and specie reserves in late 1939. It explains that Japan accelerated gold exports to procure and export commodities from the United States before the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation terminated on January 26, 1940, noting total gold exports of 2.2 billion yen since March 1937. The memorandum contrasts the Bank of Japan's published reserve of 501,287,000 yen with evidence from local banking sources and Department studies showing the reserve had actually declined to roughly 369,780,000 yen, citing temporary reporting of this lower figure by the Japan Times and Mail.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Japanese Gold Exports and Bank of Japan Reserves
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
